concept.name: Mean reversion
concept.definition: The hypothesis, and the family of strategies built on it, that asset prices or returns contain a transitory component that tends to revert toward a long-run mean, so that extreme moves are at least partially undone. Empirically, stock returns show positive serial correlation at short horizons and negative autocorrelation at long horizons, consistent with a slowly decaying transitory price component, though the effect is statistical and contested, not a law.
concept.intuition: What stretches too far from its usual level tends to snap back; mean-reversion traders buy what has fallen too far and sell what has risen too far.
concept.mechanics: Traders measure deviation from an estimated mean (moving average, fair-value model, or historical spread) and take positions expecting reversion, exiting when the series returns toward its mean. Statistically, mean reversion is tested with variance-ratio tests or modeled with mean-reverting processes such as Ornstein-Uhlenbeck.
concept.formula: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model: dX_t = theta * (mu - X_t) dt + sigma dW_t, where mu is the long-run mean, theta the speed of reversion, and sigma the volatility; variance-ratio test: VR(q) = Var(r_t^q) / (q * Var(r_t)), with VR < 1 indicating mean reversion (Poterba and Summers 1988).
concept.failure_modes: When the underlying equilibrium shifts (structural breaks, bankruptcies, regime change), 'cheap' assets keep getting cheaper; betting against strong trends produces large losses, and estimated reversion speeds are unstable out of sample.
concept.misconceptions: That prices must revert to a historical mean on a predictable schedule, or that mean reversion contradicts momentum; empirically both coexist at different horizons, and apparent reversion can reflect time-varying required returns rather than mispricing.
concept.example: A stock drops 12% in two weeks on no fundamental news while its sector is flat; a mean-reversion trader buys, expecting the gap versus its 60-day average to close, and exits after an 8% rebound.
